findings.title: The name as a devotional act
findings.claim: The focus phrase “in the name of Allah” can also be heard as an act of invocation and remembrance: 17:110 calls on Allah or al-Rahman through divine names, 7:180 commands calling on God by the beautiful names, and 73:8 commands remembering the Lord’s name and devoting oneself to Him.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries ism as a designation and Allah as the fixed divine name. The wider verses attach that same name field to calling and remembrance; those independent acts contact the focus’s bound naming relation, so the opening formula can function as devotional address and recollection.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the opening names as something enacted in the utterance: God is addressed and remembered through them.
findings.containment: The focus retains its ordinary prepositional sense, “in the name of Allah.” The wider verses supply invocation and remembrance; they do not give the focus an imperative or vocative form.

epistemic.reason: The supplied Arabic gives explicit name, calling, and remembrance relations. Their transfer to this focus is contextual, and the connection rows are nominations without target morphology or explicit source-trust labels.

findings.title: Naming at a boundary of worship
findings.claim: The focus’s name and divine epithets can also be heard against a wider boundary of unique reference and worship: 19:65 asks whether God has a namesake, 39:11 directs worship exclusively to Allah, and 43:45 asks whether gods beside al-Rahman are to be worshipped.
findings.mechanism: The focus’s ism and fixed name meet the namesake question in 19:65, while Allah and al-Rahman return in separate passages that place them at the center of worship and its rival boundary. Together these contacts let the opening naming resonate as a designation of the worshipped referent.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can perceive a devotional orientation within the names: they identify the one addressed in worship and place that address beside questions of namesakes and rivals.
findings.containment: The focus itself states no worship command or polemic. In particular, the receiving-direction note for 39:11 says the opening invocation alone does not state exclusive worship; that boundary comes from these wider contexts and does not replace the ordinary basmala reading.

epistemic.reason: The exact target Arabic supplies the namesake, exclusive-worship, and rival-worship wording. The integrated relation is contextual, target morphology is absent, and the connection records are nominations rather than final decisions.

findings.containment: The packet supplies only 27:30, which identifies the sender and gives the basmala. This does not make the S90 focus a letter or establish what follows beyond the supplied text.

findings.title: Mercy as a self-stated commitment
findings.claim: The focus’s divine mercy epithets can also be heard with the wider relation of mercy prescribed upon God Himself: 6:12 and 6:54 state that He has written mercy upon Himself.
findings.mechanism: The focus’s paired mercy adjectives carry divine mercy. In 6:12 and 6:54, the independent verb of writing or prescribing connects mercy directly to God’s own self-relation; 6:54 then places repentance and repair beside that mercy. This contact makes the epithets resonate with mercy as self-stated commitment.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can perceive the mercy names as carrying an enacted relation of commitment alongside their ordinary divine-attribute sense.
findings.containment: The focus remains a divine mercy formula. The other verses supply the self-prescription relation; they do not assert that the focus itself narrates those events or that mercy is exhausted by this formulation.

epistemic.reason: The Arabic target texts explicitly place mercy on God Himself, but the connection records provide no target morphology or source-trust labels; applying that relation to the focus is contextual.

findings.title: Mercy in reach and response
findings.claim: The focus’s mercy names can be heard in a wider relation between broad reach and human response: 7:56 pairs a command to call in fear and hope with the statement that God’s mercy is near to doers of good; 7:156 says mercy encompasses all things and is written for those who guard, give, and believe; al-Rahman also names the Lord people obey, rely on, and serve with humility and peace.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries divine mercy. The independent statements in 7:56 and 7:156 place mercy near those who do good and give it all-encompassing scope; 20:90 and 67:29 place al-Rahman beside following, obedience, belief, and reliance; 25:63 identifies humble, peaceful servants with al-Rahman. These different contacts join the divine mercy name to devotional and social responses.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the focus’s mercy names hold broad scope together with trust, obedience, and humane conduct associated with them elsewhere.
findings.containment: The focus keeps its ordinary divine-mercy sense. These contexts do not make the focus itself a command, and 7:156’s broad reach remains alongside its stated relation to those who guard, give, and believe.

epistemic.reason: Each supplied target gives explicit wording for the contact, but grouping the different responses into one global relation is interpretive. The connection records are nominations and do not include target morphology or source-trust labels.
